title: Confession
hookLine: the parent who already saw the broken lamp, waiting; Shantideva confesses to Buddhas who already know
tomorrow: can you be glad for someone who just beat you?

cards: A lamp is lying in pieces on the living room floor. The parent saw the whole thing from the kitchen doorway: the ball, the bounce, the crash. The kid doesn't know that.
So the parent waits, and the kid starts talking about how the cat was acting strange today. The parent already knows. Everybody in the room can feel that the knowing isn't the point.
They're waiting for one sentence. And that's today's puzzle, because Shantideva's confession goes to an audience that already knows everything.

teach.b: Here's the odd detail. The whole second chapter is called a confession of wrongs, and Shantideva makes it to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, with folded hands. In his own tradition, Buddhas see clearly.
They don't need the news. So why say it? Read how the chapter closes.
He asks the guides of the world to accept his wrongs as wrongs. And then: since this was not good, I will not do it again. That's the answer to the puzzle.
Confession isn't for the listener's information.
It changes the person speaking. While a wrong stays unspoken, it stays half-owned: a cat that was acting strange, a story we tell around it. Said out loud, it becomes mine, with a name and a shape.
And only a wrong with a name can get a promise attached: not again. Notice the tone, too. He confesses to beings he describes as full of compassion.
It's not a courtroom. It's the kitchen doorway, with someone who already saw and is waiting for one honest sentence.

how: Confession has a place across Buddhist practice: Theravada monks and nuns confess faults to one another regularly, and Mahayana and Tibetan practitioners recite confession texts before images of Buddhas, often with prostrations.

o: a secret ritual that wipes out all past mistakes
owning a wrong openly, as the start of change
an official written record kept by a temple

p: Buddhas and bodhisattvas, full of compassion
since it wasn't good, not again

s: Buddhist confession tells the Buddhas something they didn't know
in Shantideva's tradition the Buddhas already see. confession changes the one who speaks.
Shantideva closes his confession with a promise not to do it again
he asks the guides of the world to accept his wrongs as wrongs, and says: not again.
confession in the poem is like standing trial
he speaks to beings full of compassion. it's closer to a kitchen doorway than a courtroom.

games.q: at work you sent the wrong file to a client. your boss was copied and clearly saw. what fits Shantideva's confession?
o: say nothing; she already knows, so mentioning it is pointless.
explain why the system made it easy to send the wrong file.
tell her plainly it was your mistake, and what you'll do next time.
games.why: that she already knows isn't the point. said out loud, the mistake becomes yours, and only then can a 'not again' be attached.

practice: With a pen and paper, write one mistake you've made recently, in one plain sentence, with no excuses attached. Under it, write what you'll do differently.
Then put the pen down and sit with the page, the way you'd sit with someone who already knows.

wordCard.voice: Confession: owning a wrong openly, as the start of change. Not news for the one who hears it, but a turn for the one who says it.

orig.note: Sanskrit: declaring wrongs, confession. The name of the Bodhicaryavatara's second chapter.

carryVoice: Here's the line: said out loud, a wrong can finally be mended. That's chapter two, closed.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 2.27-2.30 (confession with folded hands to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of great compassion)
Bodhicaryavatara 2.64-2.65 (accept my wrongs as wrongs; since it is not good, I will not do it again)
